_meta.scope: Testimony, speeches, and elder voices threaded through the app. Some are archival text-only (recording technology didn't reach those survivors in time); some are audio; some are video. Each is shown with full context and attribution.
_meta.note: Where no direct audio of a specific person exists, we present the testimony as text with archival framing — not a voice actor recreation. A voice actor reading Rebecca Neugin's 1932 testimony would be a performance, not a record. We'd rather let the text stand.

rebecca-neugin-1932.speaker: Rebecca Neugin
rebecca-neugin-1932.speakerRole: Trail of Tears survivor (age ~3 at removal in 1838)
rebecca-neugin-1932.dateContext: Rebecca Neugin was in her late nineties when Grant Foreman interviewed her for the Indian-Pioneer History Collection. She was one of the last living survivors of the removal.
rebecca-neugin-1932.quote: The soldiers came and took us from our home. They first surrounded our house and then took the mother, father, and the four children. Two of the children were too small to walk, so they were put in a wagon. My mother was only allowed to bring one coat. My father wanted to fight, but my mother told him that the soldiers would kill him if he did.
rebecca-neugin-1932.shortQuote: My father wanted to fight, but my mother told him that the soldiers would kill him if he did.
rebecca-neugin-1932.attribution: Rebecca Neugin, interview with Grant Foreman, 1932
rebecca-neugin-1932.source: Grant Foreman, Indian-Pioneer History Collection, Western History Collections, University of Oklahoma Libraries
rebecca-neugin-1932.context: Neugin's memories are among the very few first-person accounts of the removal itself — she was a child when she walked the Trail of Tears, and lived long enough to be interviewed in the 1930s. One of her most-cited memories: she carried a pet duckling with her on the march and grieved to see it lost along the roadside.

junaluska-oral-tradition.speaker: Junaluska
junaluska-oral-tradition.speakerRole: Cherokee warrior who fought alongside Jackson at Horseshoe Bend
junaluska-oral-tradition.date: Oral tradition; recorded in writing in the mid-19th century
junaluska-oral-tradition.dateContext: Preserved in Cherokee oral tradition rather than contemporaneous 1814 written sources. Appears in multiple historical accounts through the 19th century.
junaluska-oral-tradition.quote: If I had known that Jackson would drive us from our homes, I would have killed him that day at the Horseshoe.
junaluska-oral-tradition.shortQuote: If I had known that Jackson would drive us from our homes, I would have killed him that day at the Horseshoe.
junaluska-oral-tradition.attribution: Junaluska, as preserved in Cherokee oral tradition
junaluska-oral-tradition.context: Cherokee tradition holds that Junaluska personally saved Andrew Jackson's life at Horseshoe Bend in 1814. Twenty-four years later, Jackson forced Junaluska's own people from their homes. Junaluska walked the Trail of Tears, then walked back to North Carolina.

nanyehi-1817.speaker: Nanyehi (Nancy Ward) and twelve other Cherokee women
nanyehi-1817.speakerRole: Nanyehi was Ghigau — Beloved Woman of Chota; as Ghigau she held the only voting seat for a woman on the Cherokee General Council.
nanyehi-1817.dateContext: Written plea from Nanyehi and twelve other women of the Cherokee Women's Council, read aloud to the Cherokee National Council by her son, shortly after the first treaty with explicit removal provisions (1817).
nanyehi-1817.quote: Your mothers and sisters ask and beg of you not to part with any more of our lands. We say you are our descendants, and must listen to our request. Keep the land for our growing children, for it was the good will of our creator to place us here, and you know our father the great president will not allow his white children to take our country away.
nanyehi-1817.shortQuote: Your mothers and sisters ask and beg of you not to part with any more of our lands.
nanyehi-1817.attribution: Nanyehi (Nancy Ward) and the Cherokee Women's Council, written plea to the Cherokee National Council, May 2, 1817
nanyehi-1817.source: Reproduced by Bill of Rights Institute, NCpedia, and Tennessee Encyclopedia
nanyehi-1817.context: Nanyehi was nearly 80 and did not appear in person. She and twelve other women of the Women's Council sent a written plea that her son read aloud to the National Council. The 1817 treaty had offered Cherokee families 640-acre reservations in the East in exchange for moving west; the women's petition helped cement the Cherokee Council's position that no more land would be sold under any terms.

john-ross-1836.speaker: John Ross
john-ross-1836.speakerRole: Principal Chief of the Cherokee Nation, 1828–1866
john-ross-1836.dateContext: Written shortly after the U.S. Senate ratified the Treaty of New Echota by one vote above the two-thirds threshold required.
john-ross-1836.quote: A spurious Delegation, in violation of a special injunction of the general council of the nation, proceeded to Washington City with this pretended treaty... We the great body of the Cherokee people, entered our solemn protest against these proceedings.
john-ross-1836.shortQuote: A spurious Delegation, in violation of a special injunction of the general council of the nation, proceeded to Washington City with this pretended treaty.
john-ross-1836.attribution: Principal Chief John Ross, open letter to the United States Senate, 1836
john-ross-1836.context: Ross collected approximately 16,000 Cherokee signatures on a petition rejecting the Treaty of New Echota — a petition more than thirty times larger than the treaty's own signatures. The Senate ratified the treaty anyway.

wilma-mankiller-success.speaker: Wilma Mankiller
wilma-mankiller-success.speakerRole: First woman elected Principal Chief of the Cherokee Nation (1985–1995)
wilma-mankiller-success.dateContext: From her memoir, written near the end of her decade as Principal Chief.
wilma-mankiller-success.quote: The secret of our success is that we never, never give up.
wilma-mankiller-success.shortQuote: The secret of our success is that we never, never give up.
wilma-mankiller-success.attribution: Wilma Mankiller, Principal Chief of the Cherokee Nation
wilma-mankiller-success.source: Wilma Mankiller and Michael Wallis, Mankiller: A Chief and Her People (St. Martin's Press, 1993)
wilma-mankiller-success.context: Mankiller survived a near-fatal 1979 car accident and a dystrophy diagnosis before leading the Cherokee Nation through a decade of rebuilding. Her name — Asgaya-dihi — is a traditional Cherokee military rank that was held by her family for generations before it became her English surname.

jerry-wolf-wikitongues.speaker: Jerry Wolf
jerry-wolf-wikitongues.speakerRole: Eastern Band of Cherokee Indians elder and storyteller
jerry-wolf-wikitongues.dateContext: Recorded by the Wikitongues language documentation project as part of their effort to preserve endangered languages around the world.
jerry-wolf-wikitongues.transcript: Cherokee spoken in the middle (Kituwah) dialect. Transcription and English translation not available for this particular recording — consult the EBCI Kituwah Preservation & Education Program for dialect-specific transcription assistance.
jerry-wolf-wikitongues.attribution: Spoken by Jerry Wolf; recorded and published by Wikitongues
jerry-wolf-wikitongues.context: Jerry Wolf was a beloved EBCI elder whose willingness to share the Cherokee language on record helped preserve the middle dialect for future generations. The recording captures 46 seconds of spoken Cherokee.

hassan-cherokee.speaker: Hassan Kiehne
hassan-cherokee.dateContext: Recorded as part of the Wikitongues language documentation project — documenting Cherokee as spoken by a younger generation of speakers.
hassan-cherokee.transcript: A Cherokee speaker in conversation with Wikitongues. Full transcription not provided by Wikitongues.
hassan-cherokee.attribution: Wikitongues volunteer Hassan Kiehne, recorded in the United States
hassan-cherokee.context: Part of Wikitongues' mission to document every living language. This recording represents Cherokee as it's spoken by a contemporary speaker — a living language, not an artifact.

michell-hicks-testimony-2025.speaker: Michell Hicks
michell-hicks-testimony-2025.speakerRole: Principal Chief of the Eastern Band of Cherokee Indians
michell-hicks-testimony-2025.dateContext: Chief Hicks testifying before the U.S. Congress on the Lumbee Fairness Act — addressing federal tribal recognition policy and its implications for Cherokee sovereignty.
michell-hicks-testimony-2025.transcript: Full Congressional testimony available via Indianz.com. Transcript excerpts available on the EBCI Council website.
michell-hicks-testimony-2025.context: Two hundred years after the Trail of Tears, a Principal Chief of the Cherokee addresses the U.S. Congress — not in defense of removal, but as a sovereign voice in federal policymaking. Chief Hicks previously served as Principal Chief from 2003 to 2015; he was re-elected in 2023.
